25.canonical: Avoid eval, and treat any data placed into an eval string as executable code.

77.canonical: Use associative arrays only when unordered key/value storage is acceptable; preserve values when expanding and sort output explicitly when presentation order matters.

79.canonical: Choose comparison operators by operand type: string operators compare strings, while -eq/-ne/-lt/-le/-gt/-ge compare integers.

91.canonical: Use here-documents and here-strings to feed inline input, quoting the delimiter for literal here-doc bodies and using <<- only when leading tabs should be stripped.

102.canonical: Use special parameters for runtime state such as the last status, background PID, argument count, script name, and positional parameters, quoting "$@" when preserving arguments.

104.canonical: Use job control deliberately for interactive jobs, knowing how process groups, backgrounding, suspension, fg/bg/jobs/disown, and terminal signals affect job lifetime and input.

106.canonical: Prefer readable scripts: use consistent indentation and style, clear long options or continuations when helpful, comments for reasoning, and quoting instead of escape clutter.

111.canonical: Commands run with & are asynchronous, and when job control is disabled their standard input defaults to a /dev/null-like source unless redirected explicitly.

114.canonical: Order case patterns from specific to catch-all, add a final * default when unmatched input should be handled, and remember that a case with no match returns success.

119.canonical: Define shell functions with valid names and compound-command bodies, knowing calls run the body with temporary positional parameters and return the body or explicit return status.

120.canonical: Inside functions, use the function positional parameters, FUNCNAME, and quoted argument forwarding to build reusable wrappers safely.

121.canonical: Use errtrace and functrace when ERR, DEBUG, and RETURN traps must propagate into functions, command substitutions, or subshells that would not inherit them by default.

129.canonical: Do not assign directly to positional or special parameters; manage positional parameters with set -- and shift.

136.canonical: Avoid broad or complicated pattern and regex matching against long strings when performance matters; test correctness and performance on realistic inputs or match smaller pieces.

138.canonical: Choose redirection operators by intent: > creates or truncates, >> appends, noclobber makes > fail unless >| is used, and combined-stream forms redirect or append stdout and stderr together.

141.canonical: Duplicate, move, open, or close file descriptors explicitly with the [n]<&word, [n]>&word, [n]<&digit-, [n]>&digit-, and [n]<>word redirection forms.

144.canonical: Use disown or disown -h when an interactive job should be removed from the jobs table or shielded from SIGHUP after the shell exits.

145.canonical: Protect dash-leading operands from option parsing by using --, ./ prefixes, quoting, escaping, or explicit dotfile handling as appropriate for the command.

156.canonical: Use printf instead of echo for reliable script-grade formatted output, treating format and argument mismatches as bugs.

179.canonical: Use indexed arrays for zero-based integer subscripts and associative arrays for string keys, creating them with declarations or compound assignments as appropriate.

183.canonical: Design prompts with safe PS syntax, bracketing non-printing terminal sequences and accounting for any later prompt expansion of dynamic fields.

201.canonical: Use the configure and make workflow for building Bash or similar source packages, treating configure errors and missing Makefiles as blockers and using staging or out-of-tree builds when needed.

207.canonical: Prefer Bash parameter expansion for routine string length, trimming, removal, case conversion, substitution, slicing, and default handling when shell patterns are sufficient.

209.canonical: Use Bash arrays for multi-value state in Bash-compatible scripts, accounting for creation, iteration, indexing, ordering, sparseness, version, and non-empty-input assumptions.

211.canonical: Create, truncate, or timestamp files intentionally; use shell redirection for simple empty-file creation or truncation when touch-specific timestamp behavior is not required.

212.canonical: Use Bash path, indirection, and terminal-escape features only when their shell and terminal assumptions are acceptable, and handle terminal capability differences or failed responses.

216.canonical: Prefer language, platform, or library APIs over direct operating-system command execution whenever they can perform the task.

221.canonical: For Java command execution, account for whether a shell is invoked and pass the executable and arguments separately rather than relying on a single command string as a safety boundary.

235.canonical: Before deleting or executing from find results, verify the result set with printing or prompts and choose safer per-file or batched execution modes deliberately.

236.canonical: Build regular expressions iteratively against valid and invalid examples, using anchors, escapes, captures, character classes, quantifiers, and locale controls to encode the intended data constraint.

237.canonical: Use grep and its variants with quoted patterns and explicit options that match the needed search semantics, output, context, recursion, filenames, line numbers, and fixed-string or regex behavior.

238.canonical: Choose text inspection and transformation tools by data shape, composing narrow tools into pipelines and escalating to awk, sed, or a programming language when the structure demands it.

242.canonical: Use in-place sed only when rewriting the target file is intended; prefer writing transformed output to a new file or using a templating tool when direct edits become risky or unclear.

244.canonical: Expose personal command shortcuts through aliases, functions, user-owned bin directories, symlinks, and PATH entries only where each abstraction fits.

250.canonical: Move from shell to a stronger programming language when the problem exceeds shell scripting complexity or maintainability limits.

252.canonical: Keep login-shell, default-shell, login-environment, and interactive startup changes minimal, tested, and placed in the appropriate user startup files unless administering all users.

259.canonical: Use version-control branches to isolate unfinished or experimental work, inspect diffs, commit deliberately, and make changes reviewable before sharing.

268.canonical: Use parameter expansion with quoting and braces for required values, alternates, defaults, substrings, arrays, cleanup, prefix introspection, and simple path text manipulation before spawning external tools.

271.canonical: Use SSH-family tools for encrypted remote login and file transfer, with explicit credentials, protected keys, host-key awareness, ports, agents, terminal options, and clean session closure.

278.canonical: Use tmux for persistent, organized, remote-friendly terminal sessions, including SSH sessions that should resume after disconnects.

279.canonical: Master tmux panes, windows, sessions, attach, detach, naming, and cleanup before adding advanced customizations such as Vim-style keys, styling, plugins, or advanced pane operations.

283.canonical: Verify the current directory, listings, hidden files, and path forms before running location-dependent commands; use absolute paths or home-directory forms intentionally.

285.canonical: Treat rm and shell deletion as permanent; preview wildcard targets and prefer interactive or nonrecursive removal unless recursive deletion is clearly intended.

298.canonical: Use here-documents for multi-line embedded input or output, quoting the delimiter to suppress body expansion and using <<- only when leading tabs should be stripped.

299.canonical: Treat special builtins as more fatal than ordinary utilities: their errors may abort a non-interactive shell, and their syntax or -- handling may differ from ordinary commands.

311.canonical: Use eval only for genuinely dynamic commands built from validated fragments, because eval performs a second round of shell parsing and can execute untrusted input.

319.canonical: Use Linux directory conventions as diagnostic hints, but take a read-only system-tour approach and verify actual contents and permissions before editing system files.

331.canonical: Sort and deduplicate with semantics that match the data, remembering uniq only removes adjacent duplicates while sort -u can sort and deduplicate together.

332.canonical: Use compression tools with awareness of file replacement, stdout modes, integrity testing, compression levels, viewing helpers, speed, and recovery behavior.

333.canonical: Use command-line mail and MIME tools for terminal or scripted notifications, choosing attachment handling when content is binary.

335.canonical: Compare and verify files with tools and checksum strength that match the question, using quiet modes in scripts and saved strong checksums for later integrity checks.

339.canonical: Signal processes with the least force that can work, escalating from normal termination to named signals, timeouts, and KILL only after ordinary termination fails.

346.canonical: Manage user accounts, shells, passwords, locks, groups, and IDs conservatively as persistent security state affecting login access and file ownership.

348.canonical: Prepare source builds safely by inspecting archives, extracting into controlled directories, reading project instructions, installing build tools, configuring prefixes when appropriate, and installing only after a successful build.

356.canonical: Treat ZFS as a separate storage stack: use stable device identifiers, manage pools and datasets through ZFS commands, enable features before relying on them, snapshot before risky changes, and treat destroy operations as irreversible.

357.canonical: Use backup and sync tools with exact source/destination semantics, dry runs, and transport choices, especially rsync for repeated attribute-preserving synchronization.

358.canonical: Treat raw device copying with dd as high risk, verifying input and output devices and media type before running as root because mistakes can destroy data.

359.canonical: Inspect host, interface, address, route, DHCP, and gateway facts with current tools, preferring iproute2 output over legacy interface tools.

373.canonical: Validate and report script arguments with positional parameters, argument counts, brace syntax, shift, script-name extraction, all-argument iteration, usage messages, and explicit exit codes.

393.canonical: Prefer repository-backed package management for ordinary software maintenance, using high-level tools for dependency-aware operations and low-level package-file installation only cautiously.

403.canonical: Use tar modes and path handling deliberately for archive creation, extraction, ownership, selective restore, incremental archives, standard streams, compression, file-list input, and SSH pipelines.

404.canonical: Quote regular expressions and choose the dialect expected by the tool, using extended syntax, grouping, alternation, and repetition only so the shell and regex engine preserve the intended pattern.

441.canonical: Create temporary files with mktemp or a safe user-local temporary directory, avoiding predictable shared-directory names and protecting shared-directory files with safe names and correct permissions.

442.canonical: Coordinate asynchronous child work with background execution, recorded PIDs when needed, and wait when parent correctness depends on child completion.

443.canonical: Use named pipes when a filesystem-visible FIFO is the right connection between separate processes, accounting for FIFO buffering and blocking behavior.
